webTitle: Trump asks ⁠US supreme court to allow construction of White House ballroom

fields.headline: Trump asks ⁠US supreme court to allow construction of White House ballroom
fields.trailText: Administration ‌asks justices to keep appeals court ​decision to halt work on hold ​while it ​prepares ‌a full ​appeal
fields.bodyText: The Trump administration has asked ⁠the ⁠US supreme court to allow construction of the president’s controversial $400m ⁠White House ballroom to proceed after an ‌appeals ‌court ordered work to halt. In a case testing Donald Trump’s presidential authority, the Washington-based US ⁠court of appeals for the District of Columbia circuit ruled last week that the controversial ‌project lacked the necessary approval from US Congress. The US president, who demolished the historic East Wing of the White House last year to make way for the planned ballroom, has repeatedly touted it as “a gift” to the US people. He and his aides have repeatedly cited national security as a benefit of its construction, too. In a filing, Trump’s administration ‌asked the supreme court justices to keep the decision by the US court of appeals for ⁠the District of Columbia circuit on hold while it prepares ‌a full appeal. “This case involves an extraordinary and unlawful injunction that will halt the ongoing construction of the integrated military complex including a totally secure ballroom space, at the East Wing of the White House, which is vitally required by national security,” D John Sauer, the solicitor general, wrote in the filing. Chief Justice John Roberts set a deadline of Tuesday for the plaintiffs challenging the project to respond. The appeals court upheld a lower court’s order blocking aboveground work on the ballroom until Congress grants its approval, but allowed construction on the underground security structure to continue. It also paused its own ruling for two weeks, until 21 August, to give the administration time to lodge its appeal to the supreme court. The government argues that “every part” of the project is “an integrated whole geared toward remedying security deficiencies and bringing critical improvements to the White House”. “The entire ballroom structure is designed to shield the military installation beneath it,” Sauer added. Trump’s administration has appealed a number of lower court decisions to the supreme court this week, in the wake of temporary injunctions over the president’s attempts to curb mail-in voting. The National Trust for Historic Preservation, which sued to block the ballroom’s construction, said on Friday: “The administration brazenly asserted to the DC Circuit Court of Appeals that even if Ballroom construction were unlawful, not even the supreme court had authority to stop it. “The administration’s transparent efforts to evade the rule of law, frustrate judicial review, and limit the availability of meaningful relief in the courts must stop here. The supreme court should deny the administration’s demand that it be allowed to continue ballroom construction while it appeals.”

webTitle: Trump’s spying on leftwing groups recalls J Edgar Hoover’s Cointelpro | Ken Roth

fields.headline: Donald Trump’s spying on leftwing groups recalls J Edgar Hoover’s Cointelpro
fields.trailText: The FBI from the 1950s to the 1970s tried to infiltrate and discredit leftist organizations. Trump seems to be repeating that sordid practice
fields.bodyText: It is bad enough that the Trump administration blocked a federal criminal investigation when an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent killed Renee Good as she was turning her car away from him in Minneapolis the past January. Just before the shooting, Good and her partner had been observing and protesting against ICE officers. Instead, it turns out the administration has been investigating progressive and even mainstream groups that have been involved in protests against Donald Trump’s sweeping deportations, according to newly released government documents. That Trump’s deportations have prompted widespread outrage is hardly surprising. The president arguably had an electoral mandate to secure the US-Mexican border but not to raid workplaces and neighborhoods to deport undocumented immigrants. Most such immigrants in the United States are now settled. They have been in the country for more than five years, and many have US-citizen children, work at regular jobs, pay taxes and are active members of their communities. Few Americans want their neighbors or work colleagues summarily deported. In January, Minnesota was a center of Trump’s deportation efforts. He deployed about 3,000 federal agents to this blue state to comb the streets in search of immigrants to deport. The public soon took to the streets in opposition, with some protesters using their phones to record detentions while others sounded the alarm that Trump’s agents were in the vicinity. Yet rather than conduct an inquiry into the deportation agents’ often-unbridled violence, the administration turned its prosecutorial sights on the protesters. In what it called “Operation Puppet Master”, it used its enormous investigative powers to pursue a vendetta against an array of groups that opposed its deportation agenda. Federal investigators justified the investigation by claiming that these groups might have provided help and money to the allegedly “violent opportunists and agitators” on the street. They also claimed that these groups provided “domestic terrorist financing”. This language parallels Trump’s directive last September expanding the definition of domestic terrorism to include using violence or intimidation to obstruct the rule of law. Even if violence or other lawlessness occasionally broke out among the protesters, it is a huge leap to suggest that civic groups were criminally complicit. Federal conspiracy law is broad but not limitless. It requires two or more people to agree to commit a federal crime and for the accused to be a part of that agreement. It would hardly be surprising that various progressive groups banded together to monitor and oppose Trump’s deportations. But those activities are protected by the first amendment to the US constitution. They are completely lawful. For the Trump administration to transform coordinated protests into a criminal conspiracy, it would have to show that the targeted groups knew the protests would obstruct federal agents “by force, intimidation or threat” and that such criminality was a purpose of their coordination. That is an enormous stretch. The role of federal prosecutor is powerful. A prosecutor can destroy a target’s life with the reputational sting and financial burden of a criminal prosecution. Before I joined Human Rights Watch, I served for more than four years in the 1980s as a federal prosecutor, mainly in New York City. My experience was that most federal prosecutors were aware of their power and tried to wield it in good faith. Trump’s criminal hounding of groups that oppose him shows no such deference to the requirements of justice. The first warning sign was that the Trump administration didn’t even use the justice department or its FBI, which traditionally pursue criminal investigations. Even though Trump has decimated the department, sparking the departure of many career officials who refused to be tainted by the president’s personal vendettas and politicized prosecutions, the administration chose instead to deploy the Department of Homeland Security. The DHS in turn issued administrative subpoenas, which do not require judicial authorization, and used other intrusive techniques to collect records and wire transfers from certain progressive groups going back three years – long before the anti-deportation protests began. That suggests what prosecutors refer to as a fishing expedition – the abuse of prosecutorial powers, in the absence of concrete evidence of wrongdoing, in the blind hope that something untoward might surface. Undercover federal investigators also spied on public meetings and even infiltrated group chats on Signal as activists discussed protests and their political opinions. Agents recorded license plate numbers to determine who was attending protest meetings. For example, at a 31 January meeting in a Minneapolis library, a homeland security undercover officer listened as supporters of a progressive climate group, the Sunrise Movement, discussed sit-ins, de-escalation tactics, and “having a police liaison and safety marshal present during events”. The agent at least had the honesty to report back that the Sunrise Movement organization focused on “peaceful” protests. However, the Trump administration has charged 15 people with obstructing federal immigration operations in Minnesota using vehicles and other objects. The 94-page indictment does not allege injuries to specific ICE officers or serious violence, but asserts that activists set up blockades around government buildings, threw chunks of ice at federal vehicles and “stalked” agents. Similar charges in parallel cases have already been dismissed or dropped at an unusually high rate. So far, none of the groups under investigation has been criminally charged, but prosecutors showed a grand jury a PowerPoint slide claiming that 18 groups were part of a conspiracy to impede Trump’s deportation agents in Minnesota. The broad investigation brings back memories of a prior example of egregious federal misconduct targeting perceived leftist groups. Under the notorious J Edgar Hoover, the FBI from the 1950s to the 1970s conducted Cointelpro to infiltrate and discredit leftist organizations, especially those that promoted Black civil rights or opposed the Vietnam war. Exposure of these outrages led to major reforms, which the Trump administration now seems determined to reverse. Many hope that the coming midterm elections in November will repudiate Trump’s lawlessness. Republicans are at risk of losing one or both houses of Congress. Yet this apparent abuse of criminal investigative powers reminds us that the presidency is powerful even without the legislative power of Congress. Fortunately, the judicial system has managed to halt much of Trump’s deportation overreaching. Even grand juries, which traditionally show enormous deference to prosecutors, have been rejecting requests to bring charges. Moreover, while politicized federal prosecutors have ignored much of the misconduct by Trump’s deportation agents, some state prosecutors have tried to pick up the ball. Yet much remains to be done as Trump seems determined to find ways to evade even adverse supreme court judgments. Exposure by journalists, protests by civic groups and outrage by the public are often the only tools we have. Responding to the Trump administration’s misconduct, Unidos MN, a human rights group in Minnesota, said that the government is “lashing out desperately in hopes of intimidating people and organizations that have shown the power of communities acting together”. This latest Trump abuse shows the importance of continuing to stand up to his lawless vision of his presidency. Kenneth Roth is a Guardian US columnist, a senior fellow at Yale University and a former executive director of Human Rights Watch. He is the author of Righting Wrongs: Three Decades on the Front Lines Battling Abusive Governments

webTitle: Tennessee’s Justin Pearson takes on America’s most contentious issues

fields.headline: Tennessee’s Justin Pearson takes on America’s most contentious issues
fields.trailText: The progressive candidate won a Democratic congressional primary after boldly staking positions on voting rights, datacenters and the US war machine
fields.bodyText: Justin Pearson made national headlines as one of the “Tennessee Three” – the state lawmakers expelled from the capitol protesting for gun control after a deadly school shooting. Three years later, the state representative won a Democratic congressional primary after boldly staking positions on some of America’s most contentious fault lines: voting rights, datacenters and the American war machine. “Republicans are responding to elected officials who stand up to billion-dollar datacenters, and the billionaires who own them. Democrats are responding to a vision of Medicare for All, ending genocide,” said Pearson. “The confluence that is happening between those issues, is [that] who profits off of war are the same people who are profiting off of polluting our communities and stealing our drinking water for their datacenters that replace our jobs.” That effort towards uniting disparate perspectives will be key in November’s midterm election, as Tennessee’s ninth district, once the state’s sole majority Black district, was split into pieces after the supreme court’s gutting of the Voting Rights Act’s second provision. The redistricting was part of a larger Trump administration effort to retain control of Congress and dilute the Black vote, especially in the south. At 31, Pearson has spent most of his life fighting for his community. In school, that meant fighting for new textbooks; then he launched a campaign to stop a crude oil pipeline from running through Black neighborhoods in his native Memphis. That was all before he was elected to represent the area in the state legislature – and then, a few months later, expelled over the protest. In the years since, Pearson has been at the forefront of a local movement against Elon Musk’s xAI, which has built two datacenters powered by soot-producing turbines concentrated in a Black neighborhood in south Memphis already suffering from environmental damage. That pollution was exposed in part through Memphis Community Against Pollution, an organization Pearson co-founded with his brother. Though the NAACP and environmental advocacy groups have fought in court to halt the usage of the turbines, the justice department got in the way, arguing the datacenter was needed during Operation Epic Fury. The effects of the Trump administration in Memphis continue to be acute: last September, Trump established a Memphis “taskforce” including 13 federal agencies and sent hundreds of federal agents into the city, with agents killing four Black men in the last 10 months. Trump claimed in his announcement that the city was “suffering from tremendous levels of violent crime” – but the week before, local police celebrated overall crime hitting a “historic” 25-year low. In July, over 1,000 people attended a rally for Pearson in response to the killings, where he was joined by congresswomen Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Summer Lee and Ayanna Pressley. “I’ve been adamant about prioritizing proximity to people who are poor, communities that are disenfranchised, who have been pushed to the bottom by systems of injustice, for years. That’s how I got my start in community organizing, that’s what I believe now as an elected official, and that is part of the reason that we are seeing a momentous amount of energy in our campaign,” Pearson said. “There’s also no denying of the zeitgeist of this moment: that people are thirsting for elected officials who are bold enough … willing, and strong enough to stand up to the status quo that has been rigged against everyday working-class people for a long time. And I think people are responding to that.” With his win, Pearson has joined the ranks of Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed and New York’s Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez as young progressive-populist upstarts sweeping primaries across the country. These candidates are running robust organizing-first campaigns in a model largely credited to Zohran Mamdani’s 2025 win as New York mayor, built on small individual donations (Pearson’s average donation was $31). The strategy echoes the 2016 Bernie Sanders presidential campaign and the rise of “the Squad” to Congress in 2018; unsurprisingly, Pearson was endorsed by both Sanders and Justice Democrats, the group that propelled Squad members Pressley, Ilhan Omar and Rashida Tlaib to office. “These primaries have shown voters of all ages are ready for next-generation leadership, and are more than willing to challenge the ageing Democratic establishment,” said David Hogg, co-founder of progressive Pac Leaders We Deserve, which endorsed Pearson on day one. “From stopping a $2bn oil pipeline to taking on the richest man in the world before most Americans even knew what a data center was to his historic protest for gun safety, he’s consistently out-organized money, power and corrupt politics.” Pearson said the numbers he brings out – including 150 people at a rally in Pulaski, the birthplace of the Ku Klux Klan – and his longtime engagement with his local community could make the change he’s calling for a reality. “It’s concerning to me that our party would try and put a box around who can be a Democrat when we are literally living in a moment in time where people are trying to put a box around what it means to be an American, what it means to be a citizen,” Pearson said. “It’s the politicos in Washington DC thinking they know what’s happening in the south or what’s happening in our communities better than we do – and they’re wrong.”

webTitle: Trump orders Pentagon to scrap modern jet launching tech on new US aircraft carrier and revert to steam catapults – as it happened

fields.headline: Trump orders Pentagon to scrap modern jet launching tech on new US aircraft carrier and revert to steam catapults – as it happened
fields.trailText: This live blog is now closed.
fields.bodyText: This concludes our live coverage of the second Trump administration for the day. Here are the latest developments: After nearly a decade of complaining about the fact that US aircraft carriers use electromagnetic catapult systems to launch fighter jets, Donald Trump directed the Pentagon to remove the modern launch systems from a new aircraft carrier and install the steam catapults he prefers. The Trump-appointed board of the Kennedy Center voted to temporarily close the building for renovations, and to inscribe the Trump’s name on the memorial Hegseth said that concerns about conditions on board the USS Abraham Lincoln are “completely misrepresented”. Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese, told reporters he asked Trump to exempt Australia from a newly announced 12.5% tariff based on a supposed failure to crack down on forced labor during a “wide-ranging call”. Newly disclosed records reveal the US government extensively spied on prominent leftwing organizations and on protesters as part of a vast operation into groups opposing the immigration crackdown in Minnesota earlier this year. The US military’s Central Command, or Centcom, posted what it called a “fact check” on social media on Thursday, accompanied by a graphic that labeled six recent reports about a mental health crisis onboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, during a record-breaking deployment at sea tied to the war with Iran, as “false” or “misinformed”. The graphic includes screenshots of six headlines, but fails to explain which news outlets published them. A review by the Guardian reveals that three of the headlines, which repeat the false claim that seven US sailors died in a brawl on the ship, were taken from Iranian media outlets based in Tehran. The text of the Centcom post complains about “rampant misreporting” from “multiple media outlets” about morale on board the aircraft carrier deployed to the Middle East, but fails to explain that half of the outlets are linked to Iran’s government. “One report alleged seven Sailors died in a brawl aboard the aircraft carrier and others have recently suggested a spike in suicidal ideations. These reports are FALSE”, the Centcom post reads. But the Pentagon fact-checkers appear to be trying to discredit well-sourced, factual reporting from two specialist US news outlets, the Navy Times and Stars and Stripes, which first reported that multiple sailors have attempted to jump overboard, by lumping those reports together with propagandistic fiction from two Iranian state-owned outlets, Mehr News and Press TV, and a third, West Asia News Agency (WANA), which says it “strives to provide foreign audiences with news from Iran with a novel view and narrative.” The Cenctom post ends by scolding the unnamed media outlets, calling their work “a disservice to our men and women in uniform and their loved ones”, reinforcing the false impression that the outlets spreading false information are American, not Iranian. The White House has released the full text of a memorandum from Donald Trump to Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, ordering a change in the construction of a new US Navy aircraft carrier, to replace the electromagnetic aircraft launch system with steam catapults. The supposed superiority of steam catapults for launching fighter jets has been an obsession of the president’s since 2017 when, he says, he was convinced by a single conversation with a Navy officer that the electromagnetic system installed in modern aircraft carriers was too complex. The presidential memorandum, titled, “Rebuilding the United States Navy and America’s Shipbuilding Industrial Base”, claims to address “a series of shipbuilding setbacks stemming from overly complex designs” for US Navy ships. Section 2 of the memo includes the order to change the construction of the USS Doris Miller, a Ford-class aircraft carrier known as CVN-81, which is already two years behind schedule: Sec. 2. Restoring Steam and Hydraulic Systems to Carriers. Within 60 days of the date of this memorandum, the Secretary of War, in consultation with the Secretary of the Navy, shall provide to the President, through the Director of the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) and the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs (APNSA), a plan on the required measures to replace the Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch System and Advanced Weapons Elevators with steam and hydraulic systems for the construction of CVN-81, including timelines and resourcing requirements. Senator Mark Kelly, a former astronaut and US Navy test pilot, is not impressed by reports that Donald Trump ordered a massive change in the construction of aircraft carriers on Thursday, forcing the Navy to scrap modern electromagnetic catapult systems to launch fighter jets, and install old-fashioned steam-powered catapults. Writing on social medial, Kelly commented: I’ve launched off the front of aircraft carriers hundreds of times, have a Master’s degree in aeronautical engineering, and am a test pilot and even I wouldn’t suggest to the Navy how to engineer specific systems on its ships. Donald Trump should stick to what he knows best — ballrooms, bankruptcy, and bullshit. Newly disclosed records reveal the US government extensively spied on prominent leftwing organizations and on protesters as part of a vast operation into groups opposing the immigration crackdown in Minnesota earlier this year. Internal investigative reports show the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) sent undercover agents to community meetings in the Twin Cities and New York, infiltrated Signal chats and obtained financial records of mainstream unions and left-leaning nonprofit groups. Nearly 30 internal law enforcement reports were released on Thursday as part of a criminal case the Department of Justice (DoJ) has filed against 15 Minneapolis protesters. The defendants are accused of a “conspiracy” to “impede” US immigration officers during the Trump administration’s surge in the region. The DHS investigative reports were disclosed by the government and submitted to the court by an attorney for one of the defendants. The records show that in January, DHS launched an inquiry called “Operation Puppet Master” to identify a “network of conspirators” organizing against US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). The operation came as community organizing against ICE was swelling in the region in response to the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti. A DHS report from February said the agency was looking into people who were “providing material support to violent opportunists and agitators”. The records suggest agents launched elaborate spying efforts targeting activists, protesters and mainstream progressive organizations opposing the Trump administration’s immigration policies. “I was shocked at the scope and the apparent lack of investigative discipline involved, but not totally surprised,” said Kevin Riach, an attorney for one of the indicted protesters, who filed the tranche of records in federal court. Speaking to reporters in Canberra, Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese, is currently describing the details of what he called “a very productive and wide-ranging call” with Donald Trump overnight in which he says he urged the US president to lift tariffs imposed on Australia. Albanese said he asked Trump to exempt Australia from a newly announced 12.5% tariff based on a supposed failure to crack down on forced labor. “The ask that I made of the president is that he consider full exemption” Albanese said. “I informed him about our record when it comes to dealing with issues such as modern slavery, the strengthening that we have put forward as well, to look and hold companies accountable for the supply chain process as well,” the prime minister added. “The president has a different position on tariffs, that he has expressed on a number of occasions over a number of years,” Albanese said. “We believe very much that tariffs are not in the interest of either the country that is having them imposed on them or the country imposting them.” “I did ask that Australia’s position, as a friend of the United States, be considered”, Albanese said before adding that Trump said he would give it some thought. The prime minister salso aid that he had expressed Australia’s view that an end to the US-Israel war on Iran was important, and said that Trump had provided him an extensive update on the war, but refused to divulge any details of that briefing. He also said that Australia supports the aim of preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. Albanese added that Trump thanked him for the work of more than 180 Australian firefighters dispatched to the US to help fight wildfires. After nearly a decade of publicly complaining about the fact that US aircraft carriers use electromagnetic catapult systems to launch fighter jets, instead of the steam-powered catapults of old, Donald Trump has reportedly directed the US Navy to remove the modern launch systems from its aircraft carriers and install the old-fashioned steam catapults he prefers, according to the Wall Street Journal and Reuters. The Journal reports that Trump signed a national security memorandum on Thursday directing the change he has had his heart set on since at least 2017, when he first described his brainwave to Time magazine. “You know the catapult is quite important. So I said, ‘What is this?’ ‘Sir, this is our digital catapult system’”, Trump told the magazine in 2017, recounting a conversation he said he had with a US Navy officer. “It sounded bad to me. Digital. They have digital. What is digital? And it’s very complicated, you have to be Albert Einstein to figure it out. And I said–and now they want to buy more aircraft carriers – I said, ‘What system are you going to be’– ‘Sir, we’re staying with digital.’ I said, ‘No you’re not. You[’re] going to goddamned steam, the digital costs hundreds of millions of dollars more money and it’s no good’”. A review of Trump’s public remarks shows that he has retold this story every year since 2017. In 2018, Trump brought it up during a Thanksgiving day phone call with the commanding officer of the USS Ronald Reagan, an aircraft carrier docked in Hong Kong at the time. In 2019, he recounted his conversation with the “catapulter” to Republican donors at a fundraiser. In 2020, as the nation was grappling with a pandemic, the tale became a regular part of Trump’s campaign speeches. In 2021, he told the story at the CPAC convention. In 2022, he shared it in a campaign speech in Texas. He repeated it on the campaign trail in Iowa in 2023. At one of his final campaign events before the 2024 election, Trump told Tucker Carlson the same story. After he returned to office in 2025, Trump brought up steam catapults during the swearing-in of Tulsi Gabbard as his director of national intelligence and then did so again in remarks to the crew of the USS George Washington, an aircraft carrier based in Japan. “We built an aircraft carrier for $19 billion, which is crazy. The price is crazy,” Trump recalled last month at the Army War College in Pennsylvania. “It had all sorts of modern day things that were all- instead of using steam for the catapults, they used electric.” “So when I went to the ship, because I came into office and the ship was way over budget, built in Newport News,” Trump said. “I said, ‘I want to meet the catapulter’, and a man came over, along with four of his assistants. And I said, ‘What’s better: electric catapult or steam?’ He’s been there for 25 years. He said, ‘Steam is better, sir. We can fix it with a hammer and a blowtorch. When the electric goes bad, I have to send to MIT to get geniuses over here.’ I said, ‘Steam is better?’ ‘Yes, sir it’s better’”. According to the Journal senior Navy and industry leaders “have resisted the move due to the enormous expense of tearing out such a complex system that was integral to the design” of the latest aircraft carriers. The board of the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts has once again voted to move forward with Donald Trump’s controversial plan to temporarily close the building for renovations, the New York Times reports, citing two people with direct knowledge of the proceedings. The decision will be subject to approval by a federal judge. In May, US district judge Christopher Cooper issued a temporary block on Trump’s demand to close the arts institution for two years of renovations, which was due to start in July after the board – mostly handpicked by the president – voted unanimously in favor. Defense secretary Pete Hegseth has said that concerns about conditions on board the USS Abraham Lincoln are “completely misrepresented”. This comes after several reports about food shortages and an intensifying mental health crisis on the vessel, that has now been deployed for more than 200 days, after it was redirected to the Middle East to assist with the military operation in Iran. More here Emily Moreno, the ex-wife of the embattled congressman Max Miller, has sued her former husband and his lawyer for uploading a picture of their infant daughter to a publicly accessible Dropbox folder as part of their custody battle. The complaint argues that Miller “recklessly published and disclosed to the world a nude image” of their daughter. The photos were part of a tranche of evidence that Miller’s team compiled in response to the domestic abuse allegations the lawmaker is facing following his divorce. More here A federal judge has dismissed ⁠a lawsuit by the Trump administration that alleged Harvard University failed to ⁠protect Jewish and Israeli students from harassment. In his ruling today, US district judge Richard ⁠Stearns in Boston said the Trump administration’s lawsuit, filed in March, had ‌not plausibly shown ‌an ongoing violation of federal civil rights ‌law on Harvard’s campus. Stearns said the government’s allegations focused largely on incidents amid protests over Israel’s war in Gaza during the 2023/24 school year, with only a handful of later incidents alleged ‌in March 2025 that were “too isolated and episodic” to support a claim of ongoing civil rights violations. Donald Trump has welcomed the court of international trade’s ruling that supports his decision to end the de minimis tariff exemption. A policy which allows people and businesses to avoid paying duties on packages and shipments below $800 that are shipped the US. The president called it a “BIG WIN”, branding the exemption one of “the most DESPICABLE loopholes in American Trade Policy”. An Michigan-based auto parts manufacturer filed the suit, arguing that it should be refunded for the tariffs it paid when Trump ended the exemption – in light of the supreme court’s decision this year which struck down the president’s sweeping tariffs under International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). The trade court, however, ruled that IEEPA “authorizes the president’s recission of the de minimis exemption”. The Kennedy Center board also reportedly voted to inscribe the Donald Trump’s name on the facade of its building, despite a federal order for his name to be removed from the signage. The New York Times reports that the board voted to add an inscription beneath the signage of the institution’s name –which stands as a memorial to John F Kennedy Jr – that reads: “Restored and Renovated by President Donald J Trump.” In May, the US district judge Christopher Cooper ordered Trump’s name to be removed from the building’s facade after the president had it added last year. Cooper ruled that the addition had been illegal, as only Congress had the authority to change the institution’s name. The center removed Trump’s name in June, but is appealing the decision. A Guatemalan immigrant detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) at a Newark, New Jersey, facility suffered a medical emergency and later died after being hospitalized, according to the Trump administration. José Chajón-Raxón is the third immigrant to die after being held at Delaney Hall, an ICE detention center that reopened in May 2025 amid the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. A nurse responded when Chajón-Raxón experienced a medical emergency and “witnessed Chajón-Raxón experiencing seizure-like activity”, according to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). Medical personnel were called, and he was transported to a hospital, the DHS said in a statement shared with the Guardian. ICE agents had arrested Chajón-Raxón before bringing him to Delaney Hall on 18 July, the agency said. Four days later, Chajón-Raxón was “released from ICE custody on July 22”, according to the agency, which did not provide further details about the circumstances of his release. Key questions about what happened next remain unanswered in the DHS account. The department did not say what occurred after Chajón-Raxón arrived at the hospital, whether he left the hospital before his death or exactly when he died. “Per ICE policy, when an individual is no longer in ICE custody then ICE will no longer be responsible for monitoring or reviewing deaths that may occur. This is common sense,” the DHS statement said. The case comes after a policy shift announced earlier this year under which the agency stopped reporting deaths occurring within 30 days after a person is released from custody. That change reversed a policy put in place by the Biden administration in 2021. Leavitt’s surprise resignation as the White House press secretary may trigger a sharp-elbowed race inside Trump world for one of the administration’s most prominent positions. Several names have circulated since Donald Trump announced that Leavitt would be stepping down at the end of the month to spend more time with her family. Here are a list of just some of the possible contenders. Stephen Cheung – Cheung currently serves as the White House communications director, and has worked closely with Leavitt throughout the second Trump administration. When he praised the outgoing press secretary for her tenure on Wednesday, Leavitt joked on social media that the pair had survived “many, many news cycles” together. Alina Habba – Habba is a loyal ally of the president who previously served as his personal lawyer before becoming the short-lived the US attorney for New Jersey. A federal judge ultimately ruled her appointment was unlawful. But Habba has been one of the president’s most vocal defenders on conservative outlets. According to the New York Post, citing sources within the administration, Habba is an early frontrunner to replace Leavitt. Anna Kelly – Kelly already works at the White House as the principal deputy press secretary, working under Leavitt. She was previously a spokesperson for Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, and before that she serves as national press secretary for the Republican National Committee. Katie Miller – As the wife of top White House aide and immigration policy architect Stephen Miller, she has a front row seat to the administration’s movements. And as an influential conservative podcast host, Miller has spent a lot of time interviewing cabinet officials and right-wing media figures. Prior to launching her podcast, Miller was a communications director for the so-called Department of Government Efficiency (Doge). She was vice-president Mike Pence’s press secretary from 2019-2021. Taylor Budowich – Budowich is a former White House deputy chief of staff, who worked alongside Miller and Dan Scavino, who left the White House last year to join the private sector. Alongside Leavitt, Budowich was one of the defendants in the case brought by the Associated Press after the outlet was banned from the press rotation for refusing to refer to the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America”. Todd Blanche, the newly confirmed attorney general, called on the justice department to work as “one team” with “one mission” in his first speech at the department headquarters in Washington DC, after his swearing-in ceremony this week. Blanche secured his nomination narrowly last week, after some Republican senators said his decisions while serving as acting attorney general gave them little confidence he would act independently. Lisa Murkowski and Susan Collins – two moderate lawmakers – cited Blanche’s decision to greenlight a $1.8bn so called “anti-weaponization fund” to compensate Donald Trump’s allies – as part of their decision to vote against his confirmation. “Everything that I do will not be the right path or the right decision,” Blanche said today. “But I do promise you this: I promise you that I will work as hard as any of you. I promise that I’ll listen to you. That I will listen to the ideas that you have, or adjustments that we need to make, and if we need to make them, I will make them.” Critics have said that Blanche’s takeover will only contribute to the justice department’s politicization in the second Trump administration, as the president continues to target his perceived political enemies. It was unclear immediately after the meeting, which was held virtually and was not public, whether the center intends to pursue the exact plan laid out in the report following the judge’s review. White House says it’s losing $19-$26bn a year in revenue as countries dodge tariffs The White House has said in a new report that countries are routing their exports through third countries to avoid US tariffs, estimating that there are tax revenue losses of $19bn to $26bn annually, the Associated Press reports. The report specifically highlights that China responded to new tariffs in 2018 by transshipping, sending their goods to other nations ranging from Mexico to Malaysia for packaging and limited assembly. That pattern made it look like US imports from China had dropped, but enabled Beijing to continue growing its manufacturing sector in ways that could challenge US factories and employment. Peter Navarro, the White House trade adviser, told reporters on a conference call that China is laundering its exports through more than 40 countries, though he claimed that the issues raised in the report were really more about other nations enabling the avoidance of tariffs. “For years, the great transshipment scam has let communist China launder its exports,” he said. The report comes ahead of a planned visit next month by Chinese president Xi Jinping, whom Donald Trump described in flattering terms during his own visit to Beijing in May. Navarro said that other nations such as India could also transship to avoid new tariffs and said that new trade frameworks pursued by the Trump administration are going to contain provisions that ensure trade partners that engage in the practice will be penalized. The report includes a range of estimates for the scale of transshipments to avoid tariffs, citing government and private sector numbers to estimate roughly $34.2bn to $303bn of goods transshipped each year. It used a central figure of $75bn worth of goods being transshipped to estimate how much in tax revenues have been lost. To address the challenge, Navarro said that US Customs and Border Protection has started to use artificial intelligence in a prototype program to stop transshipments. When an importer has been found to have falsified the origins of a good, its imports can be retroactively tariffed going back roughly a year, he said. Donald Trump’s executive order on vaccines does not change the US recommendations for the shots – but experts say it does create confusion and doubt about vaccines, which will lead to more illness and possibly deaths among children and will make it harder for families and pediatricians to protect them. The executive order was an attempt to reinstate sweeping changes to the vaccine schedule made earlier this year by Robert F Kennedy Jr, secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services and a longtime vaccine opponent – changes that were later halted by a federal judge. But an executive order can only offer guidance to agencies; it doesn’t change laws or set recommendations. Recommendations from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the federal agency that sets vaccine guidance, remain the same. “Nothing’s changed,” said Noele Nelson, a public health professor at Cornell University and former pediatrician. The primary effect of the order has been “adding unnecessary confusion” and “undermining trust in vaccines without any change in the scientific evidence”, she said. While the science and the recommendations are unchanged, “what is going to change is more people are going to be confused and scared”, said Vincent Iannelli, a pediatrician near Dallas and founder of Vaxopedia, a resource on vaccines. On Wednesday we reported the news that the Trump administration has finalized a rule to end Medicaid reimbursement for gender-affirming care. While advocates have prepared for the policy since it was proposed late last year, it is still “incredibly distressing for our community”, they added. The US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) pointed in a press release to international reviews of the medical evidence such as the Cass Review in the United Kingdom, which has been widely criticized for skewing the evidence, but it did not include the more recent landmark report from the Netherlands finding that gender-affirming care is safe and effective, and should be widely supported. The new HHS policy is “not about following the science. Legal challenges to the new rule could delay or block the policy entirely, Anafi said: “A lot of courts have recognized that these actions are based on prejudice and they’re not based on evidence – they’re actually contrary to the evidence.” If it does take effect, there are other options for providing the care. States could use their portion of Medicaid funds, not reimbursed by the US government, to cover gender-affirming care, and individuals and organizations may also ramp up mutual aid efforts. “Whenever we see restrictions on care that are based on politics and ideology, we know that patients are ultimately suffering,” Anafi said. ICE’s plan to give officers electric shock gloves draws outrage and fears of misuse Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s plan to give officers gloves that deliver painful electric shocks faced criticism Wednesday from Democratic elected officials and civil rights advocates, who called it unnecessary and cruel. The devices known as the G.L.O.V.E., which stands for Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter, are normal patrol gloves until an officer presses a button to activate its electrical mode.
